summary.text: Emanuel Cleaver is the incumbent Democratic U.S. Representative for Missouri's 5th District, first elected in 2004.

A United Methodist pastor, he served on the Kansas City City Council and as the city's first African American mayor before entering Congress, where he sits on the House Financial Services Committee and focuses on housing policy.

paragraphs.text: Cleaver was born in Waxahachie, Texas, in 1944.
He earned a bachelor's degree in sociology from Prairie View A&M University in 1972 and a Master of Divinity from St. Paul School of Theology in 1974.
He served as senior pastor of St. James United Methodist Church in Kansas City from 1973 to 2009, and Ballotpedia also lists work as a radio show host.
Cleaver served on the Kansas City City Council from 1979 to 1991 and then as mayor from 1991 to 1999, the city's first African American mayor.

According to his congressional biography, his work as mayor included economic development projects such as the 18th and Vine redevelopment, the Bruce R. Watkins Roadway and the reconstruction of Brush Creek.
He won election to the U.S. House on November 2, 2004, defeating Republican Jeanne Patterson, Libertarian Rick Bailie and Constitution Party candidate Darin Rodenberg.
KCUR reports he has won the seat 11 times.

As a new member of the House Financial Services Committee in 2009, he worked, according to his biography, on the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act's Neighborhood Stabilization Program and the Green Impact Zone in Kansas City, and on the Dodd-Frank Act, which created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

Cleaver chaired the Congressional Black Caucus during the 112th Congress (2011-2013) and, in the 117th Congress, chaired the Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing, Community Development, and Insurance.

His biography says he co-authored the Housing Opportunity Through Modernization Act in 2016, which became law, received the Harry S. Truman Good Neighbor Award in 2018 and has received five honorary doctoral degrees.
He and his wife have four children and grandchildren and live in Kansas City, and KCUR notes he delivered the opening prayer for the 2021 congressional session.
